events.title: Nelson elected
events.text: Democrat Ben Nelson won an open Senate seat, 51.0 to 48.8 percent over Don Stenberg.

events.title: Bush by 29
events.text: George W. Bush carried Nebraska by 29 points.

events.title: Bush by 33
events.text: Bush carried Nebraska again, by 33.2 points.

events.title: A Kellogg's mechanic
events.text: Dan Osborn began work as an industrial mechanic at the Kellogg's cereal plant in Omaha.

events.title: Nelson beats Ricketts
events.text: Nelson won a second term, 63.9 to 36.1 percent, over the Republican Pete Ricketts.

events.title: The first split
events.text: Barack Obama carried the 2nd District, around Omaha, by 3,370 votes: Nebraska's first split electoral vote.

events.title: Nelson retires
events.text: On 27 December Nelson said he would not seek a third term.

events.title: Fischer elected
events.text: Deb Fischer, of Valentine, beat Bob Kerrey, 57.8 to 42.2 percent.

events.title: Romney by 22
events.text: Mitt Romney carried Nebraska by 21.8 points.

events.title: Governor Ricketts
events.text: Ricketts was elected governor; he took office in January 2015.

events.title: Trump by 25
events.text: Donald Trump carried Nebraska by 25 points.

events.title: Fischer re-elected
events.text: Fischer beat Jane Raybould, of Lincoln, 57.7 to 38.6 percent; Ricketts won a second term as governor.

events.title: Biden wins Omaha's district
events.text: Joe Biden carried the 2nd District by 6.5 points; Trump carried the state by 19.1.

events.title: The Kellogg's strike
events.text: In October, Osborn, president of union Local 50G, led Kellogg's workers in Omaha out on strike.

events.title: Ricketts appointed
events.text: On 12 January Governor Jim Pillen appointed Ricketts to the seat Ben Sasse had left.

events.title: Winner-take-all stalls
events.text: In September state Senator Mike McDonnell declined to back a switch to winner-take-all electors.

events.title: Seward parade
events.text: Osborn, running for the Senate as an independent, marched in Seward's Fourth of July parade.

events.title: Fischer holds on
events.text: Fischer beat Osborn, 53.2 to 46.5 percent; Osborn ran ahead of Harris's margin in 91 of 93 counties.

events.title: Osborn carries Sarpy
events.text: Osborn carried Sarpy and Thurston counties, which Kamala Harris lost.

events.title: Ricketts elected
events.text: Ricketts won the special election for the rest of the term, 62.6 to 37.4 percent.

events.title: Harris wins Omaha's district
events.text: Harris carried the 2nd District by 4.6 points; Republican Don Bacon held its House seat.

events.title: Winner-take-all fails
events.text: On 8 April a winner-take-all bill fell two votes short of ending a filibuster, 31 to 18.

events.title: Ricketts votes yes
events.text: On 1 July Ricketts voted for the tax-and-spending law, which passed the Senate 51 to 50.

events.title: Osborn runs again
events.text: On 8 July Osborn announced a challenge to Ricketts.

events.title: Democrats back Osborn
events.text: The state Democratic chair, Jane Kleeb, said the party was supporting Osborn.

events.title: Lexington plant closes
events.text: In January Tyson closed its Lexington beef plant, cutting 3,212 jobs.

events.title: Burbank restored
events.text: On 23 March the Nebraska Supreme Court put Cindy Burbank back on the Democratic primary ballot.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 12 May Ricketts won 81 percent of the Republican vote and Burbank 90 percent of the Democratic vote.

events.title: Ricketts funds his campaign
events.text: From April to June Ricketts put $5.25 million of his own money into his campaign.

events.title: Osborn qualifies
events.text: On 16 July Osborn's petition was certified, with more than 6,000 valid signatures.

events.title: Burbank declines
events.text: On 17 July Burbank declined the Democratic nomination; the Secretary of State called it a cynical manipulation.

events.title: Marvin withdraws
events.text: On 21 August Mike Marvin left the race and endorsed Osborn; his name stays on the ballot.

events.title: The line stays empty
events.text: On 23 August Democratic leaders voted not to name a Senate candidate.

events.title: Two new parties
events.text: On 26 August the Supreme Court cleared the America First and Working People parties.

events.title: State Fair debate
events.text: On 1 September Ricketts and Osborn debated at the Nebraska State Fair in Grand Island.

events.title: Border wall recording
events.text: On 8 September a private recording of Osborn calling the border wall a symbol of racism was published.

events.title: Red Cloud recording
events.text: On 16 September a recording of Osborn's profane remarks about Trump supporters in Red Cloud was published.

events.title: Trump in Grand Island
events.text: On 5 October President Trump held a rally for Ricketts in Grand Island.

events.title: Early voting opens
events.text: In-person early voting began on 5 October.

events.title: Lean Republican
events.text: On 14 October Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race from Likely to Lean Republican.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Nebraskans choose between Osborn, Ricketts, Conboy, Richards and Marvin.

chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: Nebraska elects its senator in its own race, splits its electoral votes by district, and in 2026 there is no Democrat on the Senate ballot; in 2024 the independent Dan Osborn ran about fourteen points better against his Republican opponent than Kamala Harris did against hers. So the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Nebraska, so outer states are cut at the edge.
chartTitle: Share of the map's land area by presidential margin
